title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 20
paragraphs: After Pierre's departure that first evening, when Natasha had said to Princess Mary with a mischievous, mocking smile: "He looks just—yes, just as if he'd come out of a Russian bath, in a short coat and with his hair cropped"—from that moment something hidden and unknown to her but irresistible awoke in Natasha's soul.

Everything about her—her face, her walk, her look, her voice—was suddenly changed. To her own surprise, a force of life and a hope of happiness rose to the surface and demanded to be satisfied. From that evening she seemed to have forgotten everything that had happened to her. She never again complained about her situation, never said a word about the past, and was no longer afraid to make cheerful plans for the future. She spoke little of Pierre, but when Princess Mary mentioned him, a long-extinguished light flickered in her eyes and her lips curved in a strange smile.

The change that took place in Natasha at first surprised Princess Mary, but when she understood what it meant, it grieved her. "Can she have loved my brother so little that she could forget him so quickly?" she thought when she reflected on the change. But when she was with Natasha, she wasn't angry with her and didn't reproach her. The awakened force of life that had taken hold of Natasha was clearly so powerful and beyond her control that Princess Mary felt she had no right to reproach her, even in her own heart.
Natasha gave herself up so fully and openly to this new feeling that she didn't even try to hide the fact that she was no longer sad but bright and cheerful.
When Princess Mary returned to her room after her late-night conversation with Pierre, Natasha met her at the door.
"He's spoken? Yes? He has spoken?" she repeated.
And a joyful yet pitiful expression—which seemed to beg forgiveness for her joy—settled on Natasha's face.
"I wanted to listen at the door, but I knew you'd tell me."
However touching the look Natasha gave her seemed to Princess Mary, and however sorry she felt seeing her excitement, these words pained her for a moment. She remembered her brother and his love.
"But what can be done? She can't help it," the princess thought.
And with a sad, somewhat stern expression she told Natasha everything Pierre had said. Hearing that he was going to Petersburg, Natasha was stunned.
"To Petersburg!" she repeated, as if unable to understand.
But noticing the grieved look on Princess Mary's face, she guessed the reason for that sadness and suddenly began to cry.
"Mary," she said, "tell me what I should do! I'm afraid of being bad. Whatever you tell me, I'll do. Tell me..."
"You love him?"
"Yes," Natasha whispered.
"Then why are you crying? I'm happy for you," said Princess Mary, who—because of those tears—had already quite forgiven Natasha's joy.
"It won't be right away—someday. Just think how wonderful it will be when I'm his wife and you marry Nicholas!"
"Natasha, I've asked you not to talk about that. Let's talk about you."
They were silent for a while.
"But why go to Petersburg?" Natasha suddenly asked, and quickly answered her own question. "No, no—he has to... Yes, Mary, he has to."
